prize_parts.citation: for the quantum simulation of strongly correlated matter with ultracold atoms in optical lattices

statement.case_for: B020 is the case where a theorist's textbook model became an experiment you can look at. The Jaksch-Zoller proposal for the Bose-Hubbard model in an optical lattice, and the Greiner-Bloch observation of the superfluid-to-Mott-insulator transition, showed that atoms in light can be tuned to realise Hamiltonians that condensed-matter theorists could only approximate. Quantum-gas microscopes then let one see single sites. That says something about how strongly correlated quantum systems behave, which is a question about nature and not about technology. Two decades of independent confirmation, with quantitative agreement between theory and experiment, make it mature. After rereading the ballots I still put it first. It is also the candidate on which the most colleagues from different subfields converge (six of eight ranked it), and it is not just an AMO preference.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that this is a diffuse, still-maturing programme and not a single decisive discovery. The Mott transition is clean, but the headline payoff, an answer to an open question such as the doped Hubbard model, has not yet arrived. Five names are credited, so any trio leaves out strong contributors (Cirac, Esslinger, and Jaksch and Hansch, who are not on the list). Prior prizes on BEC (2001) and on ion and photon control (2012) narrow the novelty, and Zoller and Cirac also appear under trapped ions. If the committee wants a finished, sharply bounded result, B024 is the better fit.

responses.point: Kroll ranks the optical lattice clocks first as an instrument that redefines what can be measured. He prefers the experimentalist trio Bloch, Greiner and Esslinger for B020, and he worries that the simulation programme is still unfinished.
responses.response: I share his respect for B024. I ranked it second and consider it the cleanest and most reproduced result in the shortlist. Where we differ is on what the prize is for. The clocks are a superb measurement, but so far they give limits and not a new phenomenon, and they sit close to the 2005 and 2012 prizes. On B020 I take his allocation point seriously. Esslinger's fermionic Hubbard work is real, but the Mott observation is a joint result of the proposal and the experiment. Without the Jaksch-Zoller idea the experiment would not have been designed, so I keep one theory name. I would listen to an argument that Esslinger should replace Zoller if the committee decides the prize should be purely experimental.

responses.point: Johansson ranks circuit QED first as a distinct and natural follow-on to the 2025 prize. She also ranks optical-lattice simulation third, with Esslinger, and she states her closeness to the superconducting-circuit field.
responses.response: I appreciate her openness about closeness to the field, and the science of cQED is strong. My hesitation is timing and novelty. The 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits is recent, and giving the same platform another prize so soon would look like a run on one community, however distinct the physics. On B020 we agree on the core, and our difference over Esslinger versus Zoller is the same allocation question I discuss with Kroll. Her point that quantum simulation has not yet answered an open condensed-matter question is fair. I would answer that the observation of the Mott transition and of single-site correlations was itself the discovery, and that this does not depend on the later doped-Hubbard problem.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene first for the theory-experiment tie and the surprise of flat-band superconductivity. He regards the optical-lattice case as diffuse and notes the overlap with earlier quantum prizes.
responses.response: I find the twisted-bilayer case attractive, and the Bistritzer-MacDonald prediction followed by Jarillo-Herrero's experiment is a good theory-experiment story. I am less comfortable with its maturity. Eriksson himself and Mehlig note that the pairing mechanism of the superconductivity is unsettled, and the sample dependence worries me as a theorist who wants reproducible quantitative comparison. In optical lattices the parameters are known and the comparison with Monte Carlo and strong-coupling theory is quantitative. I agree with his point that the discovery is spread over many contributors, which is why I have narrowed it to the Mott transition and its proposal. I do not accept that diffuse means less fundamental, but he is right that the citation has to be written tightly.

responses.point: Pearce ranks IceCube first and the gamma-ray burst afterglow work second, preferring a detector-driven discovery that opens a new observational window. He also lists B020 with the experimental trio and flags the overlap with earlier cold-atom prizes.
responses.response: I agree that opening a new window is a strong criterion, and I defer to him and Danielsson on astrophysics. My concern about B052 is administrative as well as scientific. Only Halzen is credited, while the instrument and the discovery are the work of a large collaboration, and he says himself that the source associations are still at moderate significance. I cannot judge that well, but it suggests the astronomy part is less mature than B020. On the overlap with 2001 and 1997, I think the optical-lattice work is a distinct step, because it concerns interacting many-body physics and not the existence of condensation or cooling. That should be stated in the citation.

uncertainties: Which three of the five credited names for B020 best reflect the discovery, in particular Zoller versus Esslinger, and whether Cirac should be involved given the overlap with B006.
Whether the committee regards quantum simulation as a discovery about nature or as a technique, and whether it is sufficiently distinct from the 2001 and 2012 prizes.
Whether the optical lattice clocks (B024) are seen as a discovery or a technology advance, and how much weight the pending redefinition of the second should carry.
I am relying on memory for priority details such as the Jaksch-Zoller proposal and the role of Hansch, who is not on the credited list.
statement.conflict_note: My profile shows a long collaboration with Anne L'Huillier and the Lund and ETH attosecond groups, and I have worked with Reinhold Schuch and Paul Indelicato. None of these people are credited in any shortlisted entry. I know of no direct personal or institutional connection to Bloch, Greiner, Zoller, Katori, Ye, Cirac or Blatt, so no specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile. I note that my field, atomic physics, is close to several shortlisted entries, which may affect my judgement even without a formal conflict.
